# Caching and load

This page explains what the server keeps in memory between requests, how it reuses the beginning of a prompt it has
seen before, and why that reuse works well on a quiet server and less well on a busy one. It is for people who run the
server and want to understand what they see, without knowing how the model works inside. The flags it mentions are
listed in the [README](../README.md#options).

A token is a piece of text, often a short word or part of one. A prompt is the whole conversation so far, as tokens:
the system message, every question and every answer. Sizes on this page are in tokens, with K for 1,024 tokens, as the
flags write them: 512K is 524,288 tokens.

## What the model keeps while it reads

The model reads a prompt one token after another and keeps two things as it goes.

The first is the **token cache**: a small entry for each token read, which every later token looks back at. It
lives in the cards' memory and grows by one entry per token. The code and the flags call it the KV cache, as in
`--kv-tokens`.

The second is the **running state**: a summary of everything read so far, the same size however long the prompt is.
Each token changes it. It cannot be wound back: from the state after 20K tokens, there is no way to get the state
after 13K.

Both are needed to go on from where a prompt ends. The token cache alone is not enough, which is why the next
sections need checkpoints.

## The shared room for the token cache

All requests share one token cache of a fixed size, set by `--kv-tokens`. With `--slots 4 --kv-tokens 512k`, up to
four requests run at once, and together they hold at most 512K tokens. The cache is cut into pages of 4 tokens, so a
request holds whatever pages it needs, wherever they are.

When a request starts, the server holds room for its whole prompt plus the most it may write: its `max_tokens`, or
`--default-max-tokens` when it gives none. The room is held up front so that a request never runs out of space
halfway through an answer. If the room is not there, the request waits.

## Reusing the beginning of a prompt

Most prompts start the way an earlier one did. The next turn of a chat repeats the whole conversation so far and adds
a question. Agents send the same long system message and tool list at the start of every request. The part two
prompts share at their start is called their **prefix**.

Reading a prefix again would give the same token cache and the same running state as the first time, so the server
saves them and skips that work. The token cache's pages can simply be shared. The running state cannot, because the
state the server holds is the one from the end of the earlier prompt, not from the end of the prefix. So at chosen
points the server saves a copy of the running state. Such a copy, together with the token cache pages that come
before it, is a **checkpoint**.

A checkpoint has two parts, in two places:

- the copy of the running state, about 118 MB, in the computer's main memory;
- a hold on the pages of the token cache for every token before it, in the cards' memory. Those pages stay in the
  cache while any checkpoint or request still uses them.

Checkpoints are taken where a later prompt is likely to match up to:

- where each answer starts, so that the next turn of the same conversation can go on from there;
- every 16K tokens of a long prompt, so that a prompt that matches only part of the way still saves most of the work;
- at the end of a system message of 2,048 tokens or more. This one is **kept**: it is dropped only when no other
  checkpoint can be. At most two are kept at a time.

![Where a conversation is checkpointed, and how the next turn reuses it](images/caching-checkpoints.svg)

When a request arrives, the server looks for the checkpoint with the longest match to the start of its prompt. If it
finds one, it copies the saved running state back, shares the token cache pages before it, and reads only the rest.
The first token of the answer then comes after reading a few thousand tokens instead of the whole conversation.

The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger

When the last keeper left the lighthouse on Carrow Point, he took the brass telescope, two blankets and a cat, and he left behind a ledger. It was a thick book bound in green cloth, its spine cracked from forty years of being opened flat on a desk beside the window. Nobody at the harbour office thought to collect it. For almost a decade it sat in a drawer in the keeper's cottage, under a tin of matches and a folded tide table, until a girl named Maren Holt found it on a wet afternoon in March.

Maren was eleven that spring, and she had been sent to the cottage with her uncle, who had bought it cheaply from the council and meant to turn it into a place for walkers to stay. He spent the day pulling up rotten floorboards. She spent it opening every drawer and cupboard she could reach. Most of them held nothing but dust and the dry bodies of moths. The ledger was the first thing she found that seemed to want reading.

The entries began in a careful, upright hand. Each one gave the date, the hour, the direction and strength of the wind, the state of the sea, and the number of ships that had passed within sight of the light. Some days there were none. On others the keeper had counted fourteen or fifteen: colliers heading south with coal, fishing boats returning before a storm, once a grey warship that did not answer his signal. At the bottom of each page he had added a line or two about whatever else had happened. "Gannets diving off the north rocks all morning." "Lamp lit at 4.12, late, the wick needed trimming." "Letter from my sister. She says the apples have done well."

At first Maren read only those last lines, skipping the columns of numbers. But after a while she began to notice that the numbers told a story of their own. In the winters the wind came mostly from the west and the ships were fewer. In the summers there were more, and smaller, and they came closer to the shore. One year, she noticed, the count dropped sharply in October and stayed low until the following spring. The keeper had written nothing about why. She turned the pages back and forth, looking for a clue, and found only a single line in the margin of a November page: "Quiet. They say the yard at Hessel has closed."

Her uncle did not know what the yard at Hessel had been. Neither did the woman who ran the shop in the village, though she remembered her grandfather talking about the ships that used to be built there. It was the librarian in the town, a patient man with a cardigan buttoned to the throat, who finally found the answer in an old newspaper. The shipyard had built small cargo boats for coastal trade, and when it closed, two hundred men lost their work in a single week. The boats it had built kept sailing for years afterwards, but no new ones joined them, and slowly the coast grew quieter.

Maren copied the counts from the ledger into an exercise book, one year to a page, and drew a line through them in pencil. The line rose and fell with the seasons, like breathing, and then it fell and did not come back up. She showed it to her uncle, who looked at it for a long time and then said that he had not known a book of weather could hold so much.

Over the following weeks she read the whole ledger, from the first page to the last. She learned that the keeper had married late, that his wife had come to live at the point for six years and then gone back to the town, and that he had written to her every Sunday afterwards. She learned that he had once rowed out alone in a gale to a fishing boat that had lost its rudder, and that the only thing he wrote about it was the time he got back and the words "all three safe." She learned that he liked bread with caraway seeds in it, that he was afraid of thunder, and that he had kept a list, on the inside of the back cover, of every bird he had ever seen from the gallery around the lamp.

The last entry was short. It gave the date and the wind, and then it said: "Light made automatic today. Engineer very pleasant. I am to go to my sister's. The sea is the same as it was yesterday, which is a comfort."

Maren closed the book and sat for a while with it on her knees. Outside, the light had begun to turn on its own, as it had every evening for ten years, without anyone to trim the wick or write down the hour. Der alte Bahnhof von Wennerstedt liegt seit dreißig Jahren still. Die Gleise sind von Gras überwachsen, und im Wartesaal stehen noch die Holzbänke, auf denen früher Pendler auf den Frühzug in die Stadt warteten. Im vergangenen Herbst hat ein Verein aus dem Dorf beschlossen, das Gebäude zu retten. Die Mitglieder, die meisten von ihnen im Ruhestand, treffen sich jeden Samstagmorgen, um Fenster zu streichen, Dachziegel zu ersetzen und den Garten hinter dem Stellwerk in Ordnung zu bringen. Wer vorbeikommt, wird mit Kaffee aus einer großen Thermoskanne begrüßt und meistens gleich um Hilfe gebeten.

Die Pläne sind bescheiden. Im Erdgeschoss soll ein kleines Café entstehen, im ersten Stock ein Raum für Ausstellungen über die Geschichte der Strecke. Ein ehemaliger Lokführer hat seine Sammlung von Fahrkarten, Dienstplänen und Fotografien zur Verfügung gestellt. Er erzählt gern davon, wie im strengen Winter neunzehnhundertneunundsiebzig ein Zug drei Tage lang im Schnee stecken blieb und die Bauern aus der Umgebung den Reisenden Suppe und Decken brachten. Ob das Geld für alle Arbeiten reicht, weiß niemand genau.Chaque mardi, le marché couvert de Saint-Aubin ouvre ses portes avant le lever du soleil. Les premiers à arriver sont les maraîchers des villages voisins, qui déchargent leurs cagettes de poireaux, de pommes de terre et de courges sous la lumière jaune des lampes. Viennent ensuite le fromager, qui installe ses tommes sur des planches de bois, puis la boulangère, dont les pains encore tièdes remplissent l'allée centrale d'une odeur de croûte grillée. Vers huit heures, les habitués commencent à circuler entre les étals, un panier au bras, en échangeant des nouvelles du quartier.

Le marché a failli disparaître il y a quelques années. Le toit fuyait, les loyers des emplacements augmentaient, et plusieurs commerçants avaient renoncé. C'est une association de riverains qui a convaincu la mairie de financer les travaux, en organisant des réunions publiques et en recueillant plus de deux mille signatures. Aujourd'hui, les étals sont de nouveau tous occupés, et une liste d'attente s'est même formée. Le samedi, un petit orchestre山あいの小さな町、森川には、百年以上続く古い銭湯がある。木造の建物は少し傾いているが、入口ののれんは毎日きちんと掛け替えられ、番台には今も三代目の主人が座っている。営業は夕方四時から夜十時まで。仕事帰りの人や近所の老人たちが、湯気の向こうで今日の出来事を話しながら、ゆっくりと体を温めていく。

数年前、燃料費の値上がりで店を閉めることが一度は決まった。しかし、常連客の一人が町の若者に声をかけ、週末に掃除や薪割りを手伝う仲間を集めた。さらに、地元の高校生が銭湯の歴史を調べて冊子にまとめ、観光案内所に置いてもらったところ、遠くから訪れる人も少しずつ増えてきた。主人は「湯を沸かすのは一人でもできるが、続けるのは一人ではできない」と笑う。冬の夜、煙突から立ちのぼる白い煙は、今では町の人々にとって安心のしるしになっている。

先月には、町の小学校の子どもたちが社会科の授業で見学に訪れた。釜の仕組みや、薪をくべる順番、在江南的一座小城里，有一家开了四十多年的修表铺。铺子不大，只有一张工作台、一盏台灯和墙上挂满的旧钟。老板姓陈，今年已经七十岁了，每天早上八点准时开门，戴上放大镜，开始拆开顾客送来的手表。他说，每一块表都有自己的脾气，有的走得快，有的走得慢，只要耐心听它的声音，就能找到问题在哪里。

这些年，来修表的人越来越少，大多数人都用手机看时间。但仍有一些老顾客定期上门，有的拿来父亲留下的怀表，有的带着结婚时买的第一块手表。去年，一位年轻人在网上写了一篇关于这家小铺的文章，没想到吸引了不少外地游客。现在，陈师傅的孙女每到周末就来帮忙，一边学习修表，一边用相机记录下爷爷工作的样子。她说，她希望有一天能把这门手艺传下去，让更多人知道，时间也可以慢慢地被修好。

上个月，附近一所中学的老师带着学生来参观。陈师傅把一块拆开的机械表放在灯下，让孩子们看齿轮如何一格一格地转动。有个学生问他，修了一辈子表，会不会觉得无聊。他想了想说，每天都有新的问题，怎么会无聊呢。
